extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy; policymakers, landlords, and historians interested in agriculture and land tenure
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and causal principles from Adam Smith's discussion of what promotes or discourages the cultivation and improvement of land in pre-modern and early modern Europe. Includes economic, legal, social, and institutional factors affecting agricultural investment and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of cultivation for urban growth
rubrics_metrics.description: The cultivation and improvement of the country...must, necessarily, be prior to the increase of the town, which furnishes only the means of conveniency and luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Towns can only increase in proportion to the surplus produce of the country (the part beyond cultivators' maintenance). Town growth depends on agricultural surplus; towns sometimes draw subsistence from distant countries, but this does not change the general rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surplus produce as basis of town subsistence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the surplus produce of the country only...that constitutes the subsistence of the town, which can therefore increase only with the increase of the surplus produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quantity of finished manufactured work towns can sell and the materials/provisions they buy are regulated by demand from the country; neither employment nor subsistence in towns can augment except with increased demand from the country due to increased cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural preference to invest capital in land when profits are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon equal, or nearly equal profits, most men will choose to employ their capitals, rather in the improvement and cultivation of land, than either in manufactures or in foreign trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include greater visibility and command of capital in land, lower exposure to accidents (voyages, credit risks), attractiveness of country life, tranquility, independence, and the primitive inclination toward cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artisan clustering and small-town formation to serve agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificers...naturally settle in the neighbourhood of one another, and thus form a small town or village.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farmers need smiths, carpenters, masons, etc.; these artisans also need occasional mutual assistance and retailers (butcher, brewer, baker) — their mutual demand forms towns which act as continual markets for exchanging rural produce for manufactured goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of uncultivated land discourages distant-sale manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: In our North American colonies, where uncultivated land is still to be had upon easy terms, no manufactures for distant sale have ever yet been established in any of their towns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When artisans can convert surplus stock into land purchase and improvement, they become planters rather than establishing manufactures for distant markets; easy access to land draws capital away from manufacturing and trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of uncultivated land encourages manufacturing for distant sale
rubrics_metrics.description: In countries...where there is either no uncultivated land, or none that can be had upon easy terms, every artificer who has acquired more stock...endeavours to prepare work for more distant sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of land options pushes artisans to scale production and subdivide manufacturing activities, leading to gradual improvements and refinements in manufacturing processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural order of capital deployment: agriculture → manufactures → foreign commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater part of the capital of every growing society is, first, directed to agriculture, afterwards to manufactures, and, last of all, to foreign commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This order is natural because basic subsistence must be secured first; however, institutions or historical contingencies can invert this sequence, as seen in some modern European states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engrossing of uncultivated lands by few proprietors hinders division and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A great part of them was uncultivated; but no part of them, whether cultivated or uncultivated, was left without a proprietor. All of them were engrossed, and the greater part by a few great proprietors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When large tracts are monopolized and legal mechanisms (primogeniture, entails) prevent division or alienation, the possibility of small proprietors improving land is reduced and long-term cultivation may be discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primogeniture and entails prevent parceling of estates and reduce improvement incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of primogeniture hindered them from being divided by succession; the introduction of entails prevented their being broke into small parcels by alienation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primogeniture and entails were justified historically for security/power reasons but, once law and order made large estates secure, these institutions became contrary to real interest by preventing redistribution that would foster improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large proprietors often fail to improve estates
rubrics_metrics.description: It seldom happens, however, that a great proprietor is a great improver...When the establishment of law and order afforded him leisure, he often wanted the inclination, and almost always the requisite abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great proprietors may prefer ornament over profit, have extravagant household expenses, and lack the attention to 'small savings and small gains' required for profitable land improvement; they may invest in new purchases rather than improving existing holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slave labor discourages productive improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The work done by slaves, though it appears to cost only their maintenance, is in the end the dearest of any. A person who can acquire no property can have no other interest but to eat as much and to labour as little as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slaves have no property interest and therefore no incentive to increase productivity beyond subsistence; slave cultivation leads to degeneration in profitable farming compared with free labor or tenant farming that can acquire property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metayers/tenants furnished with stock by proprietor discourage tenant investment
rubrics_metrics.description: The proprietor furnished them with the seed, cattle, and instruments of husbandry...The produce was divided equally between the proprietor and the farmer...Land occupied by such tenants is properly cultivated at the expense of the proprietors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because tenants (metayers) are not required to invest their own stock, they lack incentive to invest personal savings into further improvements: improvements would largely benefit the proprietor who supplied the capital and claims half the produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security and duration of leases affect tenant willingness to invest
rubrics_metrics.description: When such farmers have a lease for a term of years, they may sometimes find it for their interest to lay out part of their capital in the further improvement of the farm...The possession...was long extremely precarious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long, secure leases encourage tenants to make improvements because they can recoup investment. Short or precarious terms, arbitrary ousting, and weak legal remedies deter investment. Legal remedies like the English action of ejectment that restore possession improve tenant security and thus investment incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary customary services and public exactions hinder improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The farmers...were anciently...bound to perform a great number of services to the landlord, which were seldom either specified in the lease, or regulated by any precise rule...The public services to which the yeomanry were bound, were not less arbitrary than the private ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unspecified, arbitrary services (road maintenance, provisioning troops at purveyor-regulated prices) and irregular oppressive taxes (tallage, taille) consume resources and discourage tenants from investing in improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes assessed on apparent stock (taille) discourage accumulation and investment
rubrics_metrics.description: The taille...is a tax upon the supposed profits of the farmer, which they estimate by the stock that he has upon the farm. It is his interest, therefore, to appear to have as little as possible, and consequently to employ as little as possible in its cultivation, and none in its improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the tax penalizes visible accumulations, farmers hide or avoid stock accumulation, preventing investment in land improvement; large taxes on farmer stock can act almost as a prohibition on employing saved capital in the farm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws restricting exportation and restraining inland commerce discourage cultivation
rubrics_metrics.description: The general prohibition of the exportation of corn, without a special licence...and the restraints which were laid upon the inland commerce...by the absurd laws against engrossers, regraters, and forestallers, and by the privileges of fairs and markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibitions on export and restrictions on trading intermediaries reduce market opportunities and prices for producers, discouraging cultivation and investment in agriculture; Smith cites these regulations as ancient policies that obstructed improvement.
